title: Great Wall of China
summary: Walls, trenches, towers and passes built by Chinese states and dynasties across northern China from about the 5th century BCE to the 17th century CE; China's 2012 survey counted 21,196 km of walls and trenches, 8,852 km of them Ming.
card: The Great Wall is many walls, not one: rammed-earth ramparts of the Warring States, the northern lines that Qin general Meng Tian joined after 221 BCE, Han reed-and-earth walls reaching the Gansu desert, and the brick-and-stone Ming wall near Beijing. A national field survey of 2006–2010, concluded in 2012, identified 43,721 surviving elements in 15 provinces. UNESCO inscribed it in 1987, yet roughly half of the Ming wall has vanished or is badly decayed, and the claim that it can be seen from the Moon is false.
what:
The Great Wall of China (Changcheng, the long walls) is the collective name for frontier fortifications built over about two thousand years, first by rival states and then by successive empires, along the northern edge of the Chinese farming world. It was never a single continuous structure. ICOMOS's 1987 evaluation traces the practice to the Spring and Autumn (722–481 BCE) and Warring States periods, when Wei walled itself against Qin in 408 BCE and Qin, Zhao and Yan, around 300 BCE, built walls facing the northern steppe. A rammed-earth wall of the state of Qi in Shandong dates to about 500 BCE. After the Qin unification of 221 BCE, Meng Tian joined the northern walls of Qin, Zhao and Yan; the Han carried the system west through the Hexi Corridor, where reed bundles in the wall have been radiocarbon dated to 132–116 BCE. The Northern Wei, the Jin and other later states built lines of their own, the Jin chiefly as trenches. The best-preserved and most visited sections, around Beijing, at Shanhaiguan on the Bohai coast and at Jiayuguan in Gansu, are Ming (1368–1644).

Its length depends on what is counted. China's State Administration of Cultural Heritage (SACH), after a field survey of 2006–2010 carried out with the national surveying and mapping agency, announced in 2012 that walls and trenches of all periods total 21,196.18 km, comprising 43,721 recorded elements in 404 counties of 15 provinces. The Ming line alone measures 8,851.8 km, of which 6,259.6 km is built wall, 359.7 km trench and 2,232.5 km natural barriers such as ridges and rivers. Older figures differ widely: ICOMOS in 1987 gave about 6,000 km for the Han wall and 5,650 km of crenellated Ming wall, and Scientific American in 2008 quoted about 7,200 km; the gap reflects which periods, branches, trenches and natural barriers each count includes.

UNESCO inscribed the wall in 1987 as serial property 438, with components at Badaling, Shanhaiguan and Jiayuguan. UNESCO's own statement of value still calls it the only human work visible from the Moon, a claim astronauts and NASA reject.

uncertainty.note: Start: the Qi wall in Shandong is dated to about 500 BCE (NPR, reporting Feinman's survey); ICOMOS traces the practice back into the Spring and Autumn period (722–481 BCE) and names the Wei wall of 408 BCE as the earliest specifically dated wall. End: the place still stands; Ming construction ended by about 1620 and the dynasty fell in 1644, after which no frontier wall-building on this scale took place.

how: Builders used what each landscape offered. Pre-Qin walls were mostly rubble or rammed earth, soil pounded in layers between wooden forms. Qin and Han walls were of earth and stone; in the gravel deserts of western Gansu, layers of reed and brushwood bundles alternate with gravel-rich rammed earth, and beacon towers of rammed loess or adobe run beyond Yumen Pass toward Aksu. The Ming first built forts, passes and signal piers (453 forts between 1368 and 1435) and only from 1437 joined them with continuous wall; in the east that wall is a loess-and-rubble core faced with brick and stone or built wholly of stone, while in the west it stayed rammed earth. The wall was one part of a defensive system. The Ming divided the frontier into nine, later eleven, military districts, with about 1,100 garrisons in a five-level hierarchy plus posts, beacon towers and relay stations. Labour came from soldiers, conscripts and convicts: the Shiji records Qin sending convicted officials to the wall, ICOMOS cites 180,000 soldier-farmers on the Gansu frontier in 102 BCE, and the Ming assigned sections to garrison troops.
why_it_matters: The walls shaped the frontier between farming states and steppe peoples for two thousand years. They helped Qin and Han hold newly conquered northern lands, guarded the Hexi Corridor through which Han power reached west (Yumen Pass is now also part of the Silk Roads World Heritage property), and in Ming times anchored a defensive system of about 1,100 garrisons with posts, beacons and relays. They never sealed the frontier: in 1550 Altan Khan's cavalry broke through near Gubeikou and plundered the countryside around Beijing for three days, and in 1644 the Qing army passed Shanhaiguan when Wu Sangui opened the gate, the Ming fell, and no large-scale wall-building followed. Because building it implied great suffering, the wall became a theme of Chinese literature from Chen Lin's ballad of about 200 CE to Du Fu's poems. Since 1961 its key sections have been protected sites, and Badaling alone received more than 76.5 million visitors between 2005 and 2015. Without the Ming rebuilding, the image most people carry, brick towers on mountain ridges, would not exist: earlier walls survive mostly as low earthen ridges, and even the Ming wall is disappearing, with only about 5.8% of its length well preserved. The 2012 survey matters too, because it replaced rough guesses with a mapped inventory that now underpins legal protection.

perspectives.holder: UNESCO statement of Outstanding Universal Value (criterion vi, retrospective statement of 2012)
perspectives.account: The wall's purpose was to protect China from outside aggression and also to keep its culture apart from the customs of peoples beyond it; its building implied suffering that became a theme of Chinese literature.

perspectives.holder: Gary Feinman (Field Museum), as reported by NPR in 2013
perspectives.account: Some of the earliest long walls, such as the Qi wall in Shandong of about 500 BCE, were most likely built to stop neighbouring Chinese states from invading one another, not to face the steppe.

perspectives.holder: Yang, Zhang and Li (2024), Heritage Science
perspectives.account: For the Ming, the number of campaigns with the Mongols tracks the surges of building, so warfare and the defensive posture toward Mongolia were the immediate cause of the wall.

perspectives.holder: Popular belief, traced by Scientific American to a 1932 Ripley's cartoon; repeated in UNESCO's statement under criterion (i)
perspectives.account: The wall is the only human work visible from the Moon.

perspectives.holder: NASA (2009) and astronauts cited by Scientific American (Neil Armstrong, Jeffrey Hoffman, Yang Liwei in 2003)

footprint.description: Line footprint from China's Great Wall resource survey (field work 2006–2010 by SACH and the National Administration of Surveying, Mapping and Geoinformation, using remote sensing, GIS, 3D scanning and photogrammetry) and the 2012 identification of 21,196.18 km of walls and trenches, split by period (pre-Qin, Qin–Han, Ming, Jin trench, other). UNESCO property 438 covers three serial components: Badaling (573.59 ha, buffer 805.58 ha), Shanhaiguan (255.36 ha, buffer 675.32 ha) and Jiayuguan (1,322.6 ha, buffer 3,319.9 ha), 2,151.55 ha in all. The survey's line data are not openly published and UNESCO notes it has not yet received georeferenced polygons, so the engine path is only as good as the placed elements below until that data is obtained.

phases.description: Spring and Autumn and Warring States walls: Qi wall in Shandong (c. 500 BCE), Wei against Qin (408 BCE), Qin, Zhao and Yan northern walls (c. 300 BCE). The 722 BCE start is ICOMOS's period bound, not a dated wall.
Qin joins and extends the northern walls of Qin, Zhao and Yan after unification (221 BCE), west along the Yellow River toward Lanzhou; completed shortly before the Han.
Han extension west through the Hexi Corridor to Yumen Pass and beacon lines toward Aksu; Gansu wall reeds dated 132–116 BCE.
Medieval phase: maintenance halts after the Han; Northern Wei build about 1,000 km in 423 and add more in the 6th century; little building under the Tang; the Jin dig a trench system.

Ming: forts and passes first (1368–1435), continuous wall from 1437, surges in 1465–1521 and 1522–1566, hollow towers 1569–1571, last new walls and large repairs to 1620, no more large-scale building to 1644.

After Wu Sangui opened Shanhaiguan to the Qing in 1644, no large-scale wall construction followed, although Shanhaiguan remained an important Qing garrison; by the 2020s over half of the Ming line had vanished or badly decayed.

Repairs begin at Juyong Pass, Badaling and Shanhaiguan in 1952; key sections protected from 1961; UNESCO listing 1987; Regulations on the Protection of the Great Wall 2006; 2005–2014 programme repairs 410 km. Most of the line remains unrestored.

materials.material: earth and stone; in western Gansu, alternating layers of reed and brushwood fascines with gravel-rich rammed earth; beacon towers of rammed loess or adobe
eastern sections: brick facing over stone and loess, or all stone (granite blocks at Mutianyu); western sections: rammed earth
earthen sections partly protected by biological soil crusts (cyanobacteria, mosses) covering about 67% of surveyed rammed-earth stretches

linear.cross_section: By period: pre-Qin and Qin–Han, a rammed-earth or earth-and-stone ridge (in western Gansu, earth layered with reed fascines); Ming east, a brick- or stone-faced wall over a rubble-and-loess core with walkway and crenellations, 1.5–4.3 m wide and up to 9.8 m high at Zhuizi Mountain, with hollow brick towers in Jizhou; Ming west, a rammed-earth wall.
